Pele Yoetz 166:1: Wine - It is written (Proverbs 23:31), "do not look at wine when it is red." Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Sanhedrin 70a) that its end is blood, for it increases transgressions and permits prohibitions, and wine does much. And it is true that there is benefit in wine when one drinks it properly, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (ibid.): whoever merits, it drinking it properly gladdens him and makes him a leader, and as Rava said (ibid.), "wine and spices make one discerning." But according to the damage that follows from it, and since a person's mind is easily enticed by it and led out of line, even if only occasionally, the loss exceeds the benefit.
Pele Yoetz 166:2: And would that the heart of the whole world be like the heart of Jonadab ben Rechab, with regard for their offspring and the generations that come after them, lest there be among them men who are not worthy, who do not know how to be careful with drinking and go out of line! And it would have been fitting for every person to be concerned about this and command his sons and his offspring after him with all firmness not to drink wine and any intoxicating substance, as the testament of Jonadab ben Rechab (Jeremiah 35:6), or to command them to drink in measure, in weight, and in proportion, and set a limit in a manner that there be no concern of going out of line. And why is there found in the world no one who is concerned about this except Jonadab ben Rechab, and we have neither seen nor heard of anyone who has done as he did? But this is the reason: for who is it whose heart dares assume that his sons and his offspring shall heed his voice and keep his mitzvah, and it might turn out that he causes them to stumble in the future into an additional prohibition, that they transgress their father's commandment - and therefore they refrain from commanding them.
Pele Yoetz 166:3: Rather, this is the mitzvah of every person upon himself: to make a fence for himself and set a limit regarding the matter of drinking, and accept upon himself with all firmness never to transgress it, so that the fear of the LORD be upon his face always, and no mishap or unfixed matter come forth from under his hand. And I say a good piece of advice: that the proper measure is that he drink two cups at one meal and not exceed this. And a sign for this matter: "two is the way of the world" (Beitzah 25b). And everything depends on what kind of person he is - whether he is strong or weak - and on the time and season, a time of gladness or a time of sadness; he may go a little beyond the two, and all his deeds shall be for the sake of Heaven (Avot 2:12).
Pele Yoetz 167:1: Childishness - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sotah 7a): childishness does much. And it is written (Proverbs 22:15), "folly is bound up in the heart of a child; the rod of discipline shall drive it far from him." And this is a mitzvah of the father toward the son: for everything he does that is not good, let him rebuke him and discipline him with reproofs for iniquity, sometimes with strikes and sometimes with blessings, and shall not show him a smiling face. And behold, just as they said (Bava Batra 21a) regarding Torah study, that at first, whoever had a father would study Torah, and whoever had no father would not study Torah, as it is written (Deuteronomy 11:19), "and you shall teach them to your sons," until they said (Bava Metzia 84b), "and shall he who has a father live, and he who has no father die?" And they instituted that they appoint teachers of children in every single city and in every single province. Likewise regarding rebuke and the guidance of children: for there are many whose fathers cannot supervise them because they are busy with their work, their labor, and their occupation, and there are some who are travelers and come home only briefly, and there are those who have a father but the teacher too cannot supervise them so much - and because of this, the children have every blemish in them and go out to bad conduct, increasing speech and jest and frivolity in the synagogue, and do not say prayers at all, and when they walk in the market they leap like rams, and the young disgrace the presence of elders and have no shame.
Pele Yoetz 167:2: And regarding all this, it is fitting to supervise and appoint leaders in every city to oversee the children. First regarding their studies: let them examine them every single week to see if they are succeeding in their studies, and if they are not succeeding, let them see whose fault the evil is - whether due to the teachers' negligence, or due to the students' lack of affection, that they do not set their minds to study - and let them discipline the one who does evil according to his own evil, each according to what is fitting for him. To the teachers, let them speak with love, open rebuke concealing hidden love, and say to them: you are our brothers - do you not know that the work of Heaven is your work, and you are day laborers? Have you not been informed of the story of Abba Chilkiyah, who did not return a greeting when Torah scholars greeted him, because he was a day laborer (Ta'anit 23a)? And likewise Rabbi Shmuel bar Shilat let thirteen years pass and did not go to see his own garden (Bava Batra 8b). You too, the truth is with you, that you have great toil - but according to the pain is the reward. And such good words that come from the heart enter the heart. And if the prevention comes from the students, let them rebuke them as is fitting for them, with words or with strikes, and let them accord honor to those who know, and rebuke and shame those who do not know. And likewise let them supervise the students, that they not sit in the marketplaces and streets, and that they not play on Sabbaths and festivals, and that they not speak in the synagogue, and that they come to pray in the synagogue morning, afternoon, and evening, and that they pray from the book, and that their lips move. And likewise let them supervise them regarding every matter of fear of Heaven, of honor, and of proper conduct.
Pele Yoetz 167:3: And it is fitting to institute a regulation in every city that the leader has authority to strike the children and discipline them as he sees fit, and no man shall protest against him. And if any person wishes to complain that the leader struck his son, let them silence him, even if it seems to him that he struck him unjustly, so that there be establishment and maintenance over the children of the school. And it is the trait of a good man to give permission to everyone and say with a full mouth, "whoever strikes and disciplines my children, I shall consider him a friend to me," for truly there is no love greater than this. And likewise it is the trait of a good man that when there is a quarrel between two children, the fathers should not become involved and should not go out to quarrel over their children's quarrel, for the children's quarrel bears no fruit and has no permanence, for they themselves make the quarrel and they themselves make peace - but the fathers' quarrel makes an impression and grows and multiplies, and it is shame and disgrace for them that they make a hateful and detestable dispute over children's quarrel.
Pele Yoetz 167:4: And there are many among the multitude of the people whose way is this (their folly is upon them - Psalms 49:14): they love their children with a bad love and show them longing and affection, and do not discipline them, and if a man draws near to discipline them and strikes them a small blow for something not good they did, immediately their father goes out to meet him for combat and makes quarrel and strife before their children, and through this the children raise their heads and increase in brazenness, and the young disgrace the presence of elders. Woe to the fathers who cause this to their sons - this is not love but enmity, and not affection but a debt owed, and not longing but an act of delusion. And the upright man who wishes to bring merit to his children's souls, even if it seems to him that they struck his only son for no wrong in his hands, shall hold gratitude toward the one who struck him in front of his son, and shall teach his sons to have shame, and not answer back to those who strike and disparage them, whether for good or for evil. And he should not worry at all about the striking of his son, for he shall not die from the blow, and the loss from division does not equal the loss of his son going out to bad conduct. Therefore, even if he wishes to protest that they not strike his son, let him choose the lesser evil, and not protest to his face, but rather, not in his presence, with pleasant speech, in a manner that there be no element of division, God forbid. And according to what this generation is, that people are very exacting regarding children, it is fitting for whoever loves peace not to strike another's child, even if he sees that they are corrupt children, God forbid, until he knows for certain that the father desires this and holds it in his favor.
Pele Yoetz 167:5: And it is also good for a man to strive with words and with gifts, and show affection, love, and longing to other people's children, for this causes an increase of love and brotherhood, peace and friendship, between a man and his fellow. And there is also a mitzvah to give peace of mind to children, who have no blemish, vanity in which there is no sin, and who are poor whose soul desires some fruit or food they see - it is fitting for father and mother and every person to fulfill their wish and their will somewhat. And with the measure a person measures, so too shall the LORD consider us a delightful child and fulfill our desires in worldly matters, even if we err - the LORD too shall grant the good in the way a person wishes, as a father has compassion on a son.
Pele Yoetz 168:1: Right - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 15b): all turns a person makes shall be only to the right side. Such as when he puts on his shoes, he shall put on the right one first, and when he puts on his clothing, and especially on Sabbath eve, he shall take both sides of the garment with his right side, encircle it around his back, and hand the left side to his left hand, and put in his right hand first, then his left hand. And likewise one must be careful with the tallit of mitzvah, that he hold both sides with his right hand, and the right hand shall hand one side to the left hand, and then wrap himself. And likewise one must be careful, when he wishes to wash his hands, to take the vessel with his right hand and hand it to the left, as one who says "after this, pour from it for me," and wash the right hand first. And likewise in everything one must be very exacting to give honor and precedence to the right, for these matters are ancient, and let him intend that "the right hand of the LORD is exalted, the right hand of the LORD does valiantly" (Psalms 118:15-16). And especially regarding the matter of lying down, one must be very careful to lie on his left side, with the right on top and the left tucked below, and whoever is not careful in this is very prone to the impurity of a seminal emission, may the Merciful One save us. And likewise, when dividing the bread portion of HaMotzi and when giving the cup of Grace after Meals to taste to those reclining, let him turn to the right side first, unless the one reclining to the left is a Torah scholar, in which case honoring the Torah takes precedence, or let him divide it into two cups. And likewise when he goes up to read from the Torah scroll, let him go up by the right way, and all such matters. And whoever is not careful and does not know his right from his left despises the matter and shall be hurt by it (Proverbs 13:13), while whoever is careful, his horn shall be exalted, the LORD his shade at his right hand.
Pele Yoetz 168:2: And of this category is that the husband should rule over his wife, and all the conduct of the house shall be by his word - for if, God forbid, his wife rules over him, woe to that woman, for she causes the left to dominate and causes strict judgments to dominate over her house, and makes an impression and a blemish above. Therefore the woman, nor her father and mother, should not wish that she rule over her husband, for this is bad for her - but if she is submissive to her husband, they shall live a sweet life, and these matters are ancient. "Length of days is in her right hand" (ibid. 3:16).
Pele Yoetz 169:1: Nursing Infants - It is found in the Holy Zohar that when a woman has relations with her husband, she should not nurse her son until about half an hour has passed, and if the child cries after a quarter of an hour, it suffices [to wait that long] because of the child's distress. And many do not know of this prohibition. Go out and learn how much they were concerned about the child's distress, to the point that they permitted an element of prohibition because of the child's distress. And certainly those women who let their nursing infants cry for a long time, until they finish their business or until they do what they wish, are destined to give judgment. And it is warned in the books that one should not nurse sons for too long a time, for it causes them to be foolish. And a sign has been established (Exodus 23:19): "the first fruits of your land you shall bring to the house of the LORD your God; you shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk." However, these are matters that have no fixed measure - if the child is weak, he should not be weaned from it too early, for that would cause him to be weak forever. And a story has already been told about a certain great man who, after several years had passed since his death, came into a difficult transmigration to suffer his punishment for having caused his own son's milk to be removed before its time so that he not be foolish, and this caused him to be weak all his days. And a nursing woman must be careful with her food, that she eat things good for milk production, and not eat coarse and bad foods, which are bad for the constitution and preparation of the offspring.
Pele Yoetz 169:2: And from the time he is nursing, his father and mother's mind must be set on raising him upon the Torah and upon service. And if one comes to teach him, let him teach at the child's side, so that his ears be attentive to words of Torah. And as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot 2:8): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya - happy is she who bore him. And they explained (Rashi, ibid.) that she who bore him caused him to be wise, for she would carry his cradle to the study house so that he hear words of Torah (as I have written below under the entry "Torah"). And in all such matters, let him do whatever is in his power to do, so that the offspring be healthy and strong, and strengthened in Torah.
Pele Yoetz 170:1: Foundation - The commentators have written that just as a building without a foundation does not endure, so too Torah study first requires a foundation - namely, that one study with the child that he be expert in faithful reading, in a clear tongue, with its vowel points and cantillation and grammar, and afterward be expert in the vernacular in all the verb conjugations in biblical, Mishnaic, and rabbinic Hebrew, in a manner that all his study be proper, each word spoken correctly, and afterward he shall study comprehension. And let him raise him in levels slowly, level after level and rung after rung. But whoever wishes to climb to the upper floor without a ladder shall fall. And how much shame comes to whoever is in the category of a Torah scholar and is not expert in reading the language properly, and does not know the vernacular according to verb conjugations - from this he comes to err when he wishes to write a letter or a book in the holy tongue, and it becomes a disgrace to his neighbors. Behold, therefore, an obligation rests upon the teachers of children to teach the earlier stages well first, until they are expert and fluent, and afterward they shall go on rising.
Pele Yoetz 171:1: Advisor - There is a mitzvah to be a good and proper advisor to whoever asks him for counsel, and he performs an act of kindness (and more is written on this under the entry "Etzah" [counsel]). However, some refrain from giving counsel because if it turns out good for him, he shall not hold gratitude toward the advisor but shall give thanks to the LORD, and if it turns out bad for him, he might curse the advisor - and therefore they say, "what is this trouble to us?" But it is not fitting for a person to be concerned about this. When they come to take counsel from him, he should not withhold good from its owner when it is in his power to do so, but rather let him clarify his intention and say: "it would have been fitting for me to withhold counsel, and I am refraining from giving counsel lest it not turn out well for you and you curse me, God forbid - but since you have come to take counsel from me, an obligation rests upon me to tell you what seems upright to me according to my own understanding, and you too are the king over your own affairs, and you shall hear all the counsel, and what is yours you shall not neglect, in a manner that if it does not turn out well for you, I shall not accept that you hold a complaint against me." Therefore, if a man is asked for counsel, he should not offer it unasked, lest his counsel not turn out well and their complaints be against him.
Pele Yoetz 171:2: And of this category is that a person should flee from being a matchmaker, for he does not know what a day may bring and what its end shall be, and it is possible for the world to be maintained through others who are matchmakers. And if his face has been asked to be a matchmaker and he cannot say "and be innocent," he should not increase in pressing and in praises as is the custom of matchmakers, but rather speak few words and say: "if it is decreed from Heaven and you have a desire for this match, do it, and the desire of the LORD in your hand shall prosper, and I shall be an agent." But if he sees his fellow wishing to do something from which mishap would certainly result, then an obligation rests upon him to inform him and advise him, because of "you shall not stand idly by the blood of your fellow" (Leviticus 19:16). All the more so if there is concern of a hint of prohibition, that he must inform him and separate him from the prohibition, for if he does not tell him, he shall bear his own iniquity. And also to his brothers and, like his father, he shall give them good counsel, and shall be sought out even unasked, for he cannot ignore it, since his brother is his own flesh - all the more so to his own offspring, that even if they act improperly by not asking him for counsel, an obligation rests upon him to have mercy on them as a father has mercy on children, and to counsel them and guide them and direct them on the good path, that they do the good and the upright in the eyes of God and man, and their deeds be proper, and it be beneficial for them, beneficial for the world, beneficial for this world and good for the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 172:1: Beauty - It is written (Proverbs 31:30): "charm is deceptive and beauty is vain; a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised." But this applies when he finds a beautiful woman who is not of good lineage or is not God-fearing - then "a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised." But if he finds beauty and fear of the LORD and lineage in one place, certainly he shall choose and draw near beauty as well, for they said (Ketubot 59b): a wife is [taken] only for beauty. And we find (Bava Metzia 84a) regarding Rabbi Yochanan, that he would sit at the gates of the mikveh, so that children as beautiful as himself be born. And Reish Lakish said to Rabbi Yochanan, "your beauty is fit for women." And it is fitting for every man to strive to take beautiful wives for his sons, so that they not set their eyes on another woman. And likewise, for this reason, he shall clothe his wife and buy her jewelry beyond what he has, so that she find favor in his eyes and he not set his eyes on another. And likewise an obligation rests upon the woman to adorn herself for her husband when she is alone with him at home more than when she goes outside to public view - for in a place where there are [other] men, it is better that she not adorn herself so much, but before her husband she shall adorn herself as much as she can, so that she find favor in her husband's eyes and he not set his eyes on another. And all the more so since these matters are ancient and allude to and make an impression in the height of the world, the place of Binah, adorning the Shechinah.
Pele Yoetz 172:2: Correspondingly, it is forbidden for a man to pursue beauty and adorn himself with adornments that women customarily make, such as curling his hair and shaving the hair under his armpits and looking in a mirror and the like. Whoever does these things transgresses "a man shall not wear a woman's garment" (Deuteronomy 22:5). But to beautify himself for the sake of Heaven is fitting and proper - such as washing his face, his hands, and his feet, and that his clothing be clean without stain and without tear, and that he be adorned in his dress, especially at the time of prayer and at the time of his engagement in Torah. These are matters that have no fixed measure, in measure and in proportion - this is the straight path.
Pele Yoetz 173:1: Sitting - We learned (Avot 2:7): whoever increases sitting increases wisdom. And the study house is called by the name "yeshivah" [sitting] to indicate that one must sit and remain there, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Eruvin 54a) on the verse (Proverbs 1:9), "and pendants for your neck" - why is the Torah compared to a necklace? To teach you: if a Torah scholar is like a necklace, which is seen and not seen [i.e., seen intermittently, going in and out of a garment], so too, if he is not seen much outside, in public view, his learning is established in his hand; and if not, his learning is not established in his hand. And it is not necessary to say [that this applies] when he does not need to go out, for if he goes out he has a transgression in his hand, for he neglects Torah and shall surely be punished - but even if he needs to go out to oversee his business, he must minimize his going out. And when he goes out, he shall be quick in his work and be content with whatever comes to his hand, in order to return to his own work, the work of Heaven, for its business is better than the business of silver. And even one who is not a Torah scholar - if the LORD has graced him that his work is done through others and he does not sit in a shop, or if he is a poor man who has no shop, let him sit all day in the study house among the sages of the city and acquire wisdom, ethics, and fear of the LORD.
Pele Yoetz 173:2: And it is a pity that there are found many (boors among the people) who have no shop, and when they have no business at all, they go all day from shop to shop, and some of them are among those who sit on street corners, and how many evils they do - one, that they neglect Torah study. And well known is the severity of the prohibition of neglecting Torah, which is equal to idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed (Yerushalmi Chagigah 1:7). And furthermore, they increase in jest and mockery and forbidden speech, and "in a multitude of words, transgression is not lacking." And whoever does these things thinks that the LORD shall not count it as an iniquity for him, for it was not given for everyone to be among those confined to the study house, only for a Torah scholar - but every other person thinks: what shall I do all day in the study house? It is to him as though he were imprisoned. And if he goes once in a great while and sits in the study house for an hour or two, he grows weary and impatient and flees from there like a child fleeing from school. Of this they said (Avot 6:2): woe to people for the affront to the Torah, for they do not value the Torah as they value money and sitting in shops and on street corners. Woe to us for the day of judgment and the day of rebuke, for according to the complete and clear truth, this is not a matter of piety but a complete law, explicit in the Mishnah, Gemara, and halachic authorities, that permission is not given to sit idle even one hour, and even a moment - even if he studied all day, he is not exempted on the day of judgment for having sat idle.
Pele Yoetz 173:3: Therefore, people of the LORD, be strong, and let us strengthen ourselves for the honor of our God, and let us have mercy on our nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, and not lose precious time. And if there are Torah scholars sitting in study in the city, let him go to the sages at every time he sits idle, and grow wise and acquire knowledge in Torah and in laws that he did not know. And if there is no Torah scholar in the city, let him sit alone and be silent, for it has been laid upon him, and let him study what he knows - such as Scripture, Mishnayot, Zohar, and the like - reviewing it again and again; let him bear it and not grow weary, until he becomes accustomed to it and it becomes sweet and pleasant to him. And indeed our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Zuta 2) that if one does not know how to study, and reviews all day the verse (Genesis 36:22), "and Lotan's sister was Timna," they give him reward as one occupied with the laws of skin afflictions and tent-defilement. And the difficulty is that the whole world already knows this and similar sayings of our holy Rabbis, but would that their hearts be set to fear and love the honored and awesome LORD and to hear the words of the sages with affection, and abandon their bad custom from now on, and merit to live and inherit good and blessing for the life of the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 174:1: Arrogance - How many things the Sages forbade because they appear arrogant, and not everyone who wishes to take the Name and perform matters of piety may do so, but rather there is a scale and just balances, and everything depends on the matter. If there is a prohibition in the thing, or neglect of a Torah-mandated mitzvah or a Rabbinic one, and most of the world is not careful about it, and he wishes to be careful and cannot do so privately, let him do it publicly, and there is no element of arrogance in this - and he should not be concerned about the mockery of the complacent, for it is better to err in this world and not be ashamed and disgraced in the World to Come. But if the consensus of the halachic authorities is to permit, and there are those who forbid, and likewise all matters of piety, he should not do it publicly, unless he is one who has acquired a good name and is established in piety, so that he knows for certain that all the people answer after him "sanctified," and there is no one who speaks disparagingly of him - but otherwise, absence is better, and he should perform these matters of piety only privately. And "he shall walk in the integrity of his heart within his house," but publicly he should not deviate from the custom of the country.
Pele Yoetz 174:2: And when he wishes to practice a good custom, let him stipulate from the outset that it be without a vow and that he shall practice it only privately. And especially one who mingles with people in business dealings and is not careful and alert in all his affairs to the point that they find no room to speak disparagingly of him, it is fitting for him to flee from conducting himself with piety publicly, for as soon as others see him, what do they say? "See the man who is dishonest [yet] recites a blessing" - and such things by which the Name of Heaven is desecrated, and the reward of the piety comes out at his own loss. And "the LORD looks at the heart" (I Samuel 16:7), and since he does it in secret, if he cannot do it publicly, Scripture credits it to him as though he had done it. And even one established in piety should not do something that the great men of the generation are not careful about publicly, so as not to cast aspersions on the earlier ones. And furthermore, they shall say, "have we not seen sages and pious men?" - this is nothing but arrogance. Therefore a good man manages his affairs with judgment, with good sense, and finds favor and good sense in the eyes of God and man, and especially before the great, if they are not careful about it, he must separate himself from matters of piety, and shall receive reward for the separation.
Pele Yoetz 175:1: Uprightness - It is fitting for a person not to stand on strict Torah law, but rather to follow what is upright, for Jerusalem was destroyed only because they stood on strict Torah law (Bava Metzia 30b), for then the Holy One, blessed be He, too judges them according to their own measure, by complete strict law, and they were found liable. And certainly whoever takes money from his fellow by strict law, not by what is upright, is destined to give judgment and is liable by the laws of Heaven - such as one who gives a deposit to his fellow and it is stolen or lost from him, that even if the law obligates him to pay, it is not upright that he repay him evil for the kindness he did for no wrong in his hands, and many such cases. But the nearby inclination holds the closed eyes, and a person does not see fault in himself, and the way of a man is straight in his own eyes. And it is fitting for whoever wishes to do the good and the upright to consult a Torah scholar, and if there is no one there to consult with, let him consult his own Maker and consider as though it were the reverse, that his fellow were demanding it of him - would it seem good and upright in his own eyes? And a person is recognized by his purse, that he should not set his eyes on money, for wealth gained hastily [without honesty] shall be diminished. And it is fitting to establish in every city men who are sensible merchants, who shall stand at the right hand of the halachic authority, and through them the judgment shall be concluded according to compromise and according to what is upright, and close to strict law but beyond the letter of the law - and then the LORD too shall grant the good beyond the letter of the law.
Pele Yoetz 175:2: And likewise, uprightness is very necessary regarding the matter of study, that it be upright, and he should not turn to a crooked and distant and forced way to maintain his own reasoning, for his study shall not be pleasing. And this trait is what increases accusation and disputes and the destruction of worlds - but every upright person who goes along and acknowledges the truth, of him it is said (Berachot 17a): happy is he whose labor is in Torah and who gives peace of mind to his Former. And these are the ones who increase peace in the world.
Pele Yoetz 176:1: Sufferings - There are several kinds of sufferings, and all are beloved, all are cherished - for if a person were to sit all his days in ease, nothing at all would be atoned for him of his sins, but sufferings scour away a person's sins (Berachot 5a; see Rashi, Nitzavim 29:14) - but one must accept them with love, knowing and recognizing the benefit in them, that they atone for his sins, and the greater benefit is that they cleanse and purify what he has blemished above and give peace of mind to his Former. Behold, therefore, the man who fears the transgressions in his own hands, and to whom it is very distressing and bitterer than death that he has blemished above, shall find it light, sweet, and pleasant to endure every kind of suffering in order to repair what he has perverted and purify what he has blemished, out of his love for his Maker, for love is as strong as death (Song of Songs 8:6), and death is chosen over life for those who fear the LORD and esteem His Name. And if it were possible and the law permitted it, they would destroy themselves knowingly and give over their own souls to death in order to repair what they perverted and purify what they blemished - all the more so when he recognizes the truth of the matter, that this whole world and its good and its evil are vanity of vanities, like a passing shadow, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Bereishit Rabbah 96:1[?]): like the shadow of a bird passing, flying in the air. And "better one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come than all the life of this world" (Avot 4:17). And therefore he should not rejoice and should not be obsessed with the good things of this world, and should not be exacting and it should not be heavy for him if he lacks things, for he shall know that they shall become luminaries.
Pele Yoetz 176:2: And behold, there are sufferings by the hand of Heaven of various kinds, harsh and gentle, which are collected from a person with or without his knowledge. And since, in any case, he must suffer even against his will, not for his own good, it is good for a man to bear the yoke and not grow weary and not grow impatient at the rebukes, but rather accept them with love, joy, and a good heart, for great is the virtue of one who rejoices in sufferings and accepts them out of love, as explained in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Berachot 5a), who said: one might think even if he did not accept them out of love it atones - the verse teaches, "if his soul makes itself a guilt offering" (Isaiah 53:10) - just as a guilt offering requires intention, so too suffering requires intention. And they further said, if he accepted them out of love, what is his reward? "He shall see offspring, prolong his days, and the desire of the LORD shall prosper in his hand."
Pele Yoetz 176:3: And in any case, for every kind of pain that befalls him, let him be accustomed to say, "this too is for the good," and "whatever the Merciful One does, He does for good" (Berachot 60b). And he should not be like fools who kick and become angry, and if they fall or stumble, speak words of insult and blasphemy - woe to them, for they inherit two Gehinnoms, that they suffer sufferings for nothing and add transgression to their sin. But those who accept everything with a good heart, their end shall be good, for whatever seems evil to a person, God has reckoned it for good - only sometimes these things are hidden from us and sometimes they are in the end revealed to us, in the manner that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Niddah 31a) regarding one whose leg was cut off and who could not go down into the ship, and began to curse his day, and in the end the ship broke apart and he began to sing, "I thank You, O LORD, for You were angry with me" (Isaiah 12:1). And it is known that a little suffering that one bears and accepts with love in this world deducts much from the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 176:4: And all the more so if he disciplines himself and afflicts his own body for the atonement of his sins - then every small amount joins to a great reckoning, and his deeds prove about him that he loves his Maker and does not spare his own body for the honor of his Maker, and therefore his Maker shall have mercy on him and remove his guilt and not stir up His wrath. And behold, the kinds of sufferings with which a person can afflict himself are many - such as afflicting himself with mortifications and fasts, and spreading sackcloth and ashes, and [rolling in] snow and thistles, and many such things, and according to the pain is the reward, that he be deducted from his sins. And the God-fearing man shall believe with complete faith that everything is as nothing compared to what he owes for having angered his Creator, and in order to purify what he has blemished and to restrain transgression and bring sin to an end - and let him not let his inclination lead him astray by telling him that he cannot bear it, for it speaks falsehood and there is nothing correct in its mouth, and whatever a man desires he can do, and all is within his power. And if the beginning is distressing, in the end, once he becomes accustomed to it, it shall be sweet to him, and he shall no longer be able to refrain from doing it - only at the beginning, strengthening is needed. And let the living take to heart how great is the honor of our Master, and how fierce is the fitting love, to the point that it is good for a man to die a thousand deaths in order to acquire the honor of Heaven, more than what he has blemished above, and to give peace of mind to his Former. And all the more so knowing that if he does not discipline himself willingly, in the end he shall be disciplined more and more in this world or the World to Come against his will, not for his own good, and he shall surely be punished also for not having had regard for the honor of his Maker and for not having striven with all his strength to purify what he has blemished, and to clean and wipe away what has soiled the King's palace with the excrement and defilement of his own sins' filth.
Pele Yoetz 176:5: However, the man who is truly weak of strength, or whose Torah is his profession, or who is a teacher of children and is concerned lest he diminish the work of Heaven, should not refrain from disciplining himself with sufferings that do not involve weakening of strength - such as lashes and wearing sackcloth, and bearing the bites of fleas and flies at times, and withdrawing his hand from pleasures and from food that is pleasant to his palate, which they have revealed to us in the name of the Ra'avad (our teacher Yonah, in his "Yesod HaTeshuvah") is considered like a fast and like a sacrifice. Who is like the wise man who knows how to do this, and such and similar things - to eat to satiety and be healthy and strong so that his sins be atoned, and every kind of pain at all that he distresses himself with joins to a great reckoning, for they said (Arachin 16b): what is an example of suffering? Such as when his shirt is turned inside out and it is a bother for him to turn it around, or when he wished to take two pennies from his purse and only one comes out, so that he needs to put his hand back in his purse. And there is a fast of hours, as Rabbi Yochanan would say (Yerushalmi Nedarim 8:1): let me be in a fast until I leave the study house. And regarding Daniel it is reckoned that he fasted in that he did not eat warm bread (Yalkut Shimoni, Daniel, ch. 10). Let the wise man hear and add learning, and let him do whatever is in his power to do for the sake of Heaven. And how good is his portion if he bears pain and suffering for the sake of performing a mitzvah - there is no atonement that multiplies more, such as bearing trouble and pain to perform it, or for its performance, or if for its performance he incurs the disgrace of a base person, and he bears it and overlooks it and is not exacting - how good is his portion and how pleasant is his lot, for they said (Yoma 23a): whoever overlooks his own traits, they overlook all his transgressions. Who is wise and shall keep these things? And the sages of ethics have already written that if they were to say to a person, "agree that your children die for the atonement of your sins," the man would tremble and say, "You, O LORD, shall guard them." And if they said, "agree that your money be consumed or that you be disciplined with harsh sufferings in your body," even for this his heart would tremble and he would say, "guard me, O God." And if so he said, by your life, in what way do you wish your sins to be atoned? Do you not know that the Holy One, blessed be He, is not lenient?
Pele Yoetz 176:6: And it is true that He is appeased through mercy and reconciled through supplications, and it is written (Hosea 14:3), "take words with you and return to the LORD" - and even if he merely contemplated repentance in his heart, he becomes a complete righteous man (Kiddushin 49b) - nevertheless, sufferings are needed to purify what he has blemished and to bring to an end and destroy the accusers created by his own sins. What is this comparable to? One who soiled and defiled the king's palace or destroyed his house, and the king became angry at him and was greatly incensed against him, to the point that he did not wish to see his face. And in the end he came to the king and wept and pleaded with him to forgive him and show him favor, and the king was reconciled to him and said to him: "behold, I show you favor and love you as before and formerly, but on condition that you trouble yourself with all your mustered strength to clean and cleanse my palace and build my house - hasten quickly, do not delay, for if you do not do so, My anger shall return." So it is with this matter, and understanding is easy for the discerning. And if a person says he does not have the strength to do this and afflict his own body, shall not God search this out?
Pele Yoetz 176:7: And all the more so, what shall he answer on the day of reckoning for not having done things that involve no weakening of strength, as stated, and many such things that are within every person's power to do - certainly he shall regret that he did not do whatever was in his power to do, his teeth shall grind and melt with no remedy, and behold, it shall be in its own time. And the best sufferings are that he press himself and bear pain to subdue his own inclination to do the will of his Former, and nullify his own will before the will of his Maker - these are sufferings of love, and according to the pain, they deduct from his sins, and he shall receive good reward for his labor.
Pele Yoetz 176:8: And a person should not think that it is enough for him and that he is exempted by what he suffers, and that the man is cleared of iniquity, for he shall believe that he owes very much for what he transgresses day by day, whether inadvertently or willingly. And what is this comparable to? Whoever owes much in a place called "truth" [i.e., the World to Come], and does not know the sum he owes, and sends there to pay through a business transaction, and does not know if he sent enough for his debt, and whether the transaction was received, and whether he profited from it, whether much or little, or whether he lost from it, or whether it went to destruction - in a manner that he must always send whatever is in his power to send, until he goes there and sees his own reckoning, perhaps there is hope that a lasting fund shall be found for him. So it is with this matter - if you have understanding, understand this. And of this it is said (Proverbs 28:14): happy is the man who is always fearful.
Pele Yoetz 176:9: And all the more so, even if he is clean and pure, it is good for a man to bear the yoke (Lamentations 3:27) and suffer sufferings for the atonement of his parents' sins, for it is fitting for the son to have mercy on his parents' souls. And likewise let him do this for the atonement of the sins of all Israel, for we are all one man. And all the more so since the man who loves the LORD is not concerned for himself but for the honor of his Maker, and thus he wishes to purify what he himself has blemished, just as what others have blemished, for his entire desire and will is to purify the blemishes above and ease the pain of the Messiah, who bears sufferings for the sins of Israel - and this is the distress of Heaven - and to give peace of mind to his Former. Behold, therefore, let him bear it and not grow weary, and not say "enough," but rather let everything seem small in his own eyes, and through this the spirit of the Omnipresent and the spirit of His creatures shall be pleased with him, for he causes good to the world, and happy is he whose labor is to give peace of mind to his Former.
Pele Yoetz 177:1: Festivals - Well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Yerushalmi Shabbat, end of ch. 15): Sabbaths and festivals were given to Israel only for engagement in Torah. And now, because of our sins, in these generations, festivals have been given only for toil and trouble, going around the streets of the city visiting from house to house, and when he returns home he is tired and weary, to the point that he does not enjoy his own feast - and it turns out that they were not festivals but days of a person's own soul-affliction, and it is possible that a person has more rest on Tisha B'Av than on a festival. And one transgression drags another - neglect of Torah and increase of idle and forbidden speech. And furthermore, exactingness, hatred, and rivalry increase if he visits one and does not visit another, or if he does not visit the poor who live in the neighborhood of the rich, or even if there is no such intention, there is exactingness - and I am also concerned about a sin, for the LORD shall contend their cause and demand their disgrace, for they are crushed and complain, saying, "if we had money, we too would be honored."
Pele Yoetz 177:2: Behold, therefore, how good and how pleasant it would be if a person could exempt himself and say "and be innocent," and sit in his own house in peace and engage in Torah according to his own knowledge, a matter in its proper time, and make his feast and sleep his sleep, and not lose his own rest, and increase his own joy, for the hour requires this - gladness and joy shall be attained, and sorrow and sighing shall flee, to fulfill what the Torah said (Deuteronomy 16:14), "and you shall rejoice in your festival." And let him take to heart things that arouse the joy of a mitzvah, not the joy of revelry like the fools who increase drinking wine and strong drink, and raise their voices in gentile melodies and melodies of lust - and granted they say they do it for the sake of a mitzvah, but this is the counsel of the evil inclination, and it is a transgression in their hands; may the good LORD atone for this.
Pele Yoetz 177:3: But those who make their paths straight shall take to heart, a matter in its proper time, why these days are remembered and observed, and what befell Israel in those days at this time, and shall go deep in pure thoughts: how good is our portion, that the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, has chosen us from among all the nations, and abundant affection is made known to us, and He has never departed from cherishing us, and has given us festivals, on which He bestows upon the nefesh, ruach, and neshamah an abundance of holiness and purity - and the Holy One, blessed be He, wished to bring merit to Israel, His chosen people, and therefore multiplied for them Torah and mitzvot, until He commanded me to rejoice on the festival, and it shall be counted a mitzvah for us, and He establishes for us reward, and many such things - is there any palate sweeter than this? Such and similar things let the living take to heart and go deep in his thought, in a manner that it is impossible not to rejoice.
Pele Yoetz 177:4: And included in the mitzvah of the day is to gladden the heart of his wife and his sons according to his ability and according to what is fitting for them, according to their own will. And they said in the Talmud (Sukkah 27b): I praise the lazy ones who do not go out of their homes on the festival, as it is written (Deuteronomy 14:26), "and you shall rejoice, you and your household." And they do not do well who feast at their friends' homes on a festival and leave their wives and children at home alone, and certainly it is distressing for them, and it is fitting for a person to nullify his own will somewhat for their will.
Pele Yoetz 177:5: And it is included in this that one gladden the hearts of the poor and needy before every festival, according to his ability. And it is known how strict they were about this in the Holy Zohar, saying that the Holy One, blessed be He, visits the poor on the festival, and if He sees that they have nothing with which to rejoice, He weeps over them. And they further said, and if a person rejoices alone and does not give to the poor, his punishment is great for not having given joy to another - of them it is written (Malachi 2:3), "and I shall spread dung on your faces, the dung of your festivals" - see there. Therefore let him not fail to give to the poor on every festival according to the blessing the LORD has given him, and let him fear and be afraid, and not be content with the little he gives, for according to the camel is the burden (Ketubot 67a[?]) - and then his heart shall rejoice and his own honor shall exult, and no evil shall befall him, and no plague shall come near his tent, and there shall be peace in his own rampart.
Pele Yoetz 177:6: And included in the mitzvah of the day is what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Megillah 4a), that Moses instituted for Israel that they inquire into the laws of a festival on the festival - and if the words of the Sages are precious and one must be careful with them, all the more so, a fortiori, is the institution of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him. And this mitzvah rests upon Torah scholars to preach publicly and give a portion to the LORD at the time of the afternoon prayer, a matter in its proper time, laws and ethics - and upon the rest of the people rests an obligation to come and hear in order to keep and to do, and they shall receive good reward for the hearing and for the doing, and thus shall it be a festival to the LORD, and the LORD shall rejoice in His works.
Pele Yoetz 178:1: Settled Mind - A settled mind is very necessary for engagement in Torah and for the service of the blessed Name, and especially for us, orphans of orphans, whose heart is not with us - it is enough for us to have any trouble at all to distract us from the service of the blessed Name. Behold, therefore, it is fitting for a person to seek settlement and flee greatly from scattering of the soul - that is, the scattering of his money and similar troubles of merchants - and "better a dry morsel with tranquility than" a heart troubled and pained and constantly fearful. And "whoever finds this city difficult should go to another city" (Bava Metzia 75b) to find rest for his own soul and seek a resting place that would be good for him for the service of his Creator. And if he has some necessary business, let him hasten to do it well beforehand in order to free his mind from this trouble, so that he have one less trouble upon him. And it is likewise good for a man that whatever he wishes to remember, whether of matters of Heaven or matters of the world, he should immediately write it down as a reminder, so that he not be troubled with having to remember to write it down lest he forget - for once he has written it, he need not keep it in his mind.
